content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with their planners and content experts, have disclosed that they have no financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. Presentations will not include discussions of unlabeled uses of products or investigational uses of products, except for the off-label use of rabies vaccines in certain animal species for which no licensed rabies vaccine exists. In cases where these species are used in settings involving public contact, consultation with a veterinarian regarding the off-label use of rabies vaccines is recommended. The cover of the report features several images: public health officials collecting samples at a petting zoo following an outbreak, a girl feeding a giraffe at a circus petting zoo, young children observing hatching chicks, a girl touching a fox at an Alaskan animal exhibit, and an image of handwashing after animal contact. These images highlight the educational and entertainment opportunities provided by fairs, educational farms, petting zoos, and schools. The National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians (NASPHV) acknowledges the positive benefits of human-animal interactions but emphasizes that inadequate understanding of disease transmission and animal behavior can increase the risk of infectious diseases, rabies exposures, injuries, and other health problems, particularly among children. Zoonoses, or diseases transmitted between animals and humans, are of particular concern when they result in widespread illness. Between 1991 and 2005, the number of enteric disease outbreaks associated with animals in public settings increased. Since 1996, approximately 100 human infectious disease outbreaks linked to animals in public settings have been reported to the CDC. While eliminating all risks from animal contact is not feasible, the report provides recommendations to minimize associated diseases and injuries. NASPHV advises local and state public health, agricultural, environmental, and wildlife agencies to use these recommendations to establish guidelines or regulations to reduce the risk of disease from human-animal contact in public settings. Managers of venues such as animal displays, petting zoos, animal swap meets, pet stores, zoological institutions, nature parks, circuses, carnivals, educational farms, livestock-birthing exhibits, fairs, childcare facilities, schools, and wildlife photo opportunities should consult with veterinarians, public health officials, or other professionals to reduce disease transmission risks. Although not specifically addressed in this report, the general principles and recommendations are applicable to these settings. NASPHV periodically updates its recommendations to prevent diseases associated with animals in public settings. The 2009 guidelines emphasize risks associated with baby poultry, reptiles, and rodents in public settings and incorporate information about aquatic animal zoonoses. Enteric (intestinal) diseases pose the highest risk for human illness from animals in public settings. Healthy animals can harbor human enteric pathogens, many of which have a low infectious dose. Outbreaks of enteric diseases among visitors to fairs, farms, and petting zoos are well-documented, with pathogens such as Escherichia coli O157:H7, Salmonella species, Cryptosporidium species, and Campylobacter species being implicated. The primary mode of transmission for enteric pathogens is the fecal-oral route. Animal fur, hair, skin, and saliva often harbor fecal organisms, and transmission can occur through petting, touching, feeding, or being licked by animals. Contaminated animal bedding, flooring, barriers, environmental surfaces, and clothing can also facilitate transmission. Illness has also resulted from fecal contamination of food, including raw milk and water. Removing ill animals, especially those with diarrhea, is necessary but insufficient to protect animal and human health, as animals carrying human enteric pathogens often show no signs of illness and can intermittently shed organisms, contaminating the environment. Some pathogens can persist in the environment for months or years. Laboratory testing limitations mean that culturing fecal specimens or identifying infected animals might reduce but cannot eliminate transmission risks. Antimicrobial treatment of animals cannot reliably eliminate infection, prevent shedding, or protect against reinfection. Treatment can prolong shedding and contribute to antimicrobial resistance. Factors such as stress from transportation, confinement, crowding, and increased handling can increase pathogen shedding in animals. Young animals, often used in petting zoos and educational programs, have a higher prevalence of certain enteric pathogens. Shedding of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) and Salmonella organisms is highest in the summer and fall, coinciding with the peak season for traveling animal exhibits, agricultural fairs, and petting zoos. Human factors and behaviors, particularly in children, increase the risk of infection. Children are especially attracted to animal venues but are at higher risk for serious infections. Farm residents might have some acquired immunity to certain pathogens, but livestock exhibitors have become infected with E. coli O157:H7 during fair outbreaks. Facility layout and maintenance can influence infection risk. Factors such as inadequate handwashing facilities, structural deficiencies in temporary food service facilities, inappropriate visitor flow, and incomplete separation between animal exhibits and food preparation or consumption areas increase risk. Contaminated or inadequately maintained drinking water and sewage or manure disposal systems also contribute to risk. Outbreaks and lessons learned include multiple instances of E. coli O157:H7 infections linked to animal contact at fairs, petting zoos, and other public settings. Risk factors include direct animal contact, inadequate handwashing, and environmental contamination. For example, in a Pennsylvania outbreak, 51 people became ill after visiting a dairy farm, with eight developing hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). The same strain of E. coli O157:H7 was isolated from cattle, patients, and the farm environment. In a Colorado zoo outbreak, 65 cases of Salmonella enterica serotype Enteritidis infections were associated with touching a wooden barrier around a Komodo dragon exhibit. Handwashing significantly reduced illness risk. Environmental contamination can result in disease transmission even without direct animal contact. For example, an Oregon county fair outbreak of E. coli O157:H7 infections was associated with visiting an exhibition hall housing goats, sheep, pigs, rabbits, and poultry. Illness was not linked to touching animals or their pens, eating, or inadequate handwashing but was likely caused by contaminated dust. Pathogens such as E. coli O157:H7 can persist in the environment for extended periods, as demonstrated in outbreaks where the organism was recovered from environmental sources weeks or months after events. Additional health concerns include injuries, rabies exposure, and infections other than enteric diseases. Injuries associated with animals in public settings include bites, kicks, falls, scratches, stings, and crushing injuries. Rabies exposure can occur through contact with rabid mammals, requiring extensive public health investigations and medical follow-up. Although no human rabies deaths from public animal contact have been reported, thousands of people have received rabies postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) after exposure to potentially rabid animals. Other infections associated with animal contact include bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic infections. Animal bites frequently require extensive treatment or hospitalization. Pathogens such as Pasteurella species, Francisella tularensis, Staphylococcus species, Streptococcus species, Capnocytophaga canimorsus, Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease), and Streptobacillus moniliformis (rat-bite fever) are associated with animal bites. Certain monkey species kept as pets or used in public exhibits can carry simian herpes B virus, which can cause fatal meningoencephalitis in humans. Skin contact with animals can also pose public health concerns. For example, ringworm outbreaks have been linked to contact with infected animals. Aquatic animals and their environments have been associated with cutaneous infections, such as Mycobacterium marinum infections among fish tank owners. Ectoparasites and endoparasites can also pose risks when humans interact with exhibit animals. Proper veterinary care, husbandry, and handwashing reduce these risks. Zoonotic pathogens can be transmitted through contact with reproductive fluids, aborted fetuses, or newborns from infected animals. Diseases such as Q fever, leptospirosis, listeriosis, brucellosis, and chlamydiosis can be acquired through contact with reproductive materials. For example, a Q fever outbreak involving 95 confirmed cases and 41 hospitalizations was linked to goats and sheep giving birth at petting zoos in indoor shopping malls. Indoor birthing exhibits might pose an increased risk for Q fever.
